newsitem.title: USA: "Pennies from Heaven" sparks debate in Miami.
newsitem.headline: "Pennies from Heaven" sparks debate in Miami.

text.p: A mad scramble for money by people in a poor, black district of Miami after a security truck spilled its assets has prompted some soul searching on Friday in a city notorious for crime and corruption.

Dozens of people in Overtown, a rundown inner city neighbourhood, scooped up cash and coins that literally rained down when a Brink's armoured security truck, believed to be carrying $3.7 million, flipped on a highway overpass on Wednesday.

Commentators and media were having a field day debating the morality of the looting. Liz Wild, a popular talk show host on WPLL-FM's Planet Radio, called their actions dishonest and undignified. Many callers to her morning show agreed.
However, a black Overtown resident who gave his name as Reggie, said on Friday that people there were so deprived their actions were justified.
"You don't understand. You (are) just white, rich," he told Wild. "Try coming to live in Overtown for a week -- you wouldn't last one hour." He said he had picked up $200 in quarters.
Reggie was followed by a woman caller who said Overtown residents complained too much about their lot. "Why is that if we go down to Overtown we get mugged. What about that?" she asked.
The Miami Herald, meanwhile, was conducting a telephone poll asking readers what they would do if they found a bag containing $10,000 from an overturned security truck.
The choices were: turn it in because it is the right thing to do; turn it in because you are worried you would get caught; keep it and feel guilty, or keep it and feel no guilt at all.
Herald humorist Dave Barry thought the incident was good news for Miami, which recieves plenty of bad publicity.

"The best part is the way the citizens responded. They did not riot, they did not become violent ... instead they came together, local residents and passing motorists alike working towards the common goal of snorking up as much of the money as possible ... People working together! For a common cause!" Barry said.
"When word gets out there's money spilling onto our streets, the tourists will flock to this town like palmetto bugs to an unguarded hostess twinkie," he added.

Miami police failed to see the humour and said a crime is a crime. On Thursday, they gave people a 48-hour amnesty to return the hundreds of thousands of missing dollars. Lt. Bill Schwartz said they were "appealing to people's morals" to return the money.
A police spokesman said that by late on Friday morning, no money had been turned in.
